lines.note: Vanare names a married man's mistress; melius recommends the form Vuanari. The latter is a Japanese alternative in upright type, and ho- continues as homem below.

runs.text: mem caſado. Palaura de que vſa algũa gente

lines.note: Completes homem casado, a married man, and begins the usage qualification. The tilde is over the u of algũa; the word is not expanded or modernized.

runs.text: baixa de Ximo: a propria palaura he Vuanari.

lines.note: The entry attributes Vanare to low-status usage in Ximo and calls Vuanari the proper expression. Both Ximo and the final Vuanari occur within the italic Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Caixa em q̃ metem eſcudelas de arroz.

lines.note: Wanbako is a box holding bowls of rice. The abbreviation q̃ is visible over q and remains unexpanded, while eſcudelas denotes the bowls rather than loose rice.
Wankot is equated with udebone, the arm bone. The checked final t in Vancot belongs to the historical Sino-Japanese form and is not expanded to a modern syllable.

runs.text: Peixe aßi chamado que dizẽ come gente.

lines.note: Wani is described as a fish said to eat people. This wording is preserved without imposing a modern zoological identification; the abbreviated dizẽ means 'they say'.
Waniashi denotes crooked or splayed feet, matched by Portuguese pes zambros. No accent is supplied to Pes where none is established in the print.
Waniguchi is described as a small bell rung before sacred figures. The sentence continues on the next physical line with the objects before which it is sounded.
Completes the bell's setting: before the kami and Buddhist images. Camis and Fotoques are Japanese religious terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation, with the printed plural endings preserved.

runs.text: Vanrei. Reiuo cayeſu. l, Fenreiuo ſuru.

lines.note: Wanrei means returning a courtesy, explained by rei wo kaesu or henrei wo suru. Tor- begins the Portuguese tornar on the next row; the alternatives remain separate printed expressions.

runs.text: nar a viſitar com algum preſente, ou retorno.

lines.note: Completes tornar a visitar: paying a return visit with a present or reciprocal offering. This is the social-return sense of wanrei, not simply turning around.

Wanriki is arm strength, paraphrased as kaina no chikara. The small damaged mark over a is retained as an abbreviation tilde in Vãriqi; the following govanriqi also supports the nasal reading. NINJAL's Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510 (Ohshima and Aida, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), corroborates the lexical identification after scan inspection. The worn pilcrow introduces the example Deos no govanriqi.
Completes Deos no gowanriki, here God's strength and power. Deos is used within the Japanese example, and the respectful go- form supplies the unabbreviated vanriqi sequence.
Wappa is a servant boy or young attendant. The short Portuguese definition identifies the service role without requiring a modern slang interpretation.

runs.text: Adu. Modode dar grita, ou fazer

lines.note: Wappato is introduced as an adverb describing a shout or noisy outburst. The printed Modode is kept together; the second coordinated action continues below.
Traquinada completes the noisy-commotion gloss; wappato wameku illustrates shouting or clamouring. The example retains the initial v spelling of wameku.
Wake is leftover rice, explained by amaru ii. The terminal I- begins Portuguese Item below and belongs to the italic explanatory text, not to the Japanese headword.

runs.text: tem, Outra qualquer couſa de comer q̃ ſobeja.

lines.note: Completes Item and broadens the sense to any leftover food. The abbreviated q̃ is retained exactly rather than expanded to que.
Wake, wakuru, waketa is the verb 'divide' or 'separate'. The printed abbreviated principal parts are preserved, and Vt introduces the group-dividing example below.
Ninjuu wo wakuru means dividing the people into groups. The Portuguese prints a space in a gente; Cõ- begins the following grammatical observation across the line break.

runs.text: munmente ſe ajunta eſte verbo às raizes de al-

lines.note: The note says this verb is commonly attached to the stems of other verbs. The scan supports raizes, with an i, rather than the OCR rarzes; the final al- continues into alguns.
Completes alguns outros and supplies mooshi wakuru, to explain with distinctions. The initial letter of vaquru is v, matching the preceding verb and the visible type, rather than OCR y.
The translation specifies speaking with distinction and clarity. Qi- begins the next Japanese compound, qiqivaquru, divided at the physical line end.
With Qi- above, this is kikiwakuru: hearing and understanding or distinguishing what is heard. The divided Japanese word remains on its two physical rows.
The noun wake is division or separation. Vaqemo- begins wake mo nai, the following expression about speech whose distinctions or meaning cannot be understood.
Completes wake mo nai koto wo yuu, saying things without an intelligible distinction or sense. The caron on yǔ is visible and is retained.
Completes the explanation as things not well understood or distinguished. A new example begins wake ga and continues with contrasting negative and affirmative predicates below.
Wake ga kikoyenu and kikoyeta contrast not being understood with having become clear. The capital Q has a broad swash but belongs to Qicoyeta; the OCR inserted an internal word space after it.

runs.text: bẽ a couſa, ou terſe bem entẽdida, & diſtincta.

lines.note: Completes the two interpretations: the matter is not well understood, or is understood distinctly. The scan retains the abbreviation bẽ and separates bem entẽdida; neither form is modernized.

runs.text: Quinhão, ou porção de qualquer couſa.

lines.note: Wakebun is a share or portion of something. The paired Portuguese nouns specify the allotted-part sense rather than an abstract reason.

runs.text: O que pertence acada hum na repar-

lines.note: Wakekuchi is the amount belonging to each person in a distribution. The close printed acada remains joined, and repar- continues as repartição below.

runs.text: tição de algũa couſa como deſpojos, prata do

lines.note: Completes repartição and gives spoil and money from a game as examples of distributed property. Prata do continues into jogo on the next row.
Jogo completes the example of game money. Wakekuchi wo toru introduces taking one's share, and To- continues as tomar on the following row.

runs.text: mar cada hum ſua parte ſeparada, ou repar-

lines.note: Completes tomar: each person takes a separate part, or one distributed by someone else. Repar- continues into repartida rather than beginning a new entry.
Completes repartida por outro, allocated by another person. The brief continuation remains an independent physical row.

runs.text: Quinhão que cada hum toma porſi.

lines.note: Wakedori is the share each person takes for himself. The abraded middle of the headword is confirmed by the repeated Vaqedoriuo on the next row.
Wakedori wo suru is dividing shares or each taking his own share. The Portuguese coordination continues below and belongs with this example.

Completes taking one's own share; enlargement supports quinhão rather than OCR quinbão. At the far right, the isolated parenthesis and eruas are a displaced completion of the next entry's matos, ou. Their physical position on this row is preserved rather than moved into Vaqeide.

Wakeide means emerging from among thickets or herbs. Eruas is printed at the far right of the preceding physical row; the text is retained there with an explicit placement marker. The abbreviation dãtre is not expanded.
Wakeiri means entering or forcing a way through something. The final en- continues as entre, specifying what one passes through below.
Completes entre gente, matos: through people, thickets, and similar obstacles. Teki no naka- begins the example of breaking through the midst of enemies.
Completes teki no naka ye wakeiru, forcing a way into the enemy's midst. The Portuguese Rõper retains its printed abbreviation tilde and historical pollo meyo spelling.
Wakemayoi describes wandering astray through mountains or difficult routes. The two abbreviated forms visibly use circumflex o, not a caron.

Completes the definition as wandering lost along bad roads. The scan shows the anomalous four-letter runs, with no secure i or tilde; the clear ruins on c2-l001 supplies a same-page comparison. The missing vowel is not silently supplied.

runs.text: Eſtremadura da couſa que ſe parte,

lines.note: Wakeme is the dividing boundary or parting in something. Eſtremadura is one printed word, not the OCR's Eſtrema dura; the following hair example clarifies the sense.

runs.text: ou diuide, como dos cabellos que eſtão diuididos

lines.note: The gloss continues with a thing divided, such as parted hair. The scan supports diuide, with u, rather than OCR dicide, while retaining the historical u/v spelling.
Completes the example as hair separated into two parts. This is the final body row of column 1, with the lower rule visible beneath it.
Wakekitari means coming through mountains or difficult roads. The final ruins includes a narrow s immediately beside the right rule, omitted by the OCR's ruim.
Completes the difficult-roads gloss and begins yama, or no wo wakekitaru, coming through mountains or fields. The Japanese verb is physically divided after vaqe-.
Qitaru completes wakekitaru. The Portuguese repeats coming through mountains and fields, with co- continuing into como below.

runs.text: mo por antre as eruas, ou matos.

lines.note: Completes como and specifies passage among herbs or thickets. Antre remains the historical spelling printed here, rather than being normalized to entre.

runs.text: De baixo do braço, ou ſouaco. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Waki first denotes the region beneath the arm or armpit. The abbreviated Itẽ introduces a separate regional temporal use on the next row.

runs.text: No Ximo, A pos algũa couſa, ou de pois de a-

lines.note: The entry identifies a Ximo usage meaning after something or after finishing it. Printed A pos and de pois remain spaced; the final a- begins acabar.
Completes acabar alguma cousa. Dangi no wa- begins the example for the time after a sermon, with waki divided across the row boundary.
Completes dangi no waki and gives go-missa no waki as the alternative, after a sermon or Mass. Prega- begins pregação on the following row.
Completes pregação and its comparison with Mass, then adds wakidachi no mizu as another expression using waki. The next line explains the depth of the water.
The water reaches the armpits. This explains wakidachi no mizu as a measure of depth, not water originating in the armpits.

runs.text: Repreſentador da obra, ou o que ſae di-

lines.note: Waki is described as a performer who comes out before the other figures to explain the play. The last letter of ſae is e rather than OCR c; the worn Repreſentador remains legible as the actor designation.

runs.text: ante das figuras no auto a dar razão do que ſe

lines.note: Completes diante and describes appearing before the other characters in the play to explain what will be represented. The relative clause continues onto the next row.
Completes what is to be performed, then introduces waki-noo or waki no noo. The damaged Portuguese initial is r in repreſentar, not OCR t.

runs.text: Primeiro acto em que começão a repreſe-

lines.note: Completes waki no noo, glossed as the first act in which the story begins to be performed. The middle of repreſe- is abraded; the OCR's internal space is not a word boundary. A tiny mark above the final e is too weak to establish an abbreviation tilde, so the unmarked e is retained provisionally before tar below.

runs.text: tar a hiſtoria dalgum auto, ou tragedia.

lines.note: Completes the damaged representar form and the explanation of performing a play's or tragedy's story. Tragedia is faint on the right but supported by its surviving letters; no new theatrical entry begins here.
Waki, waku, waita means sawing wood. Ki wo begins the object phrase; the swashed capital Q belongs to Qiuo without the OCR's internal space.

Completes ki wo waku, a Ximo usage, and contrasts the Cami expression ki wo hiku. X. is an upright regional label; Cami is embedded in the Portuguese statement, with the printed Camiſe spacing preserved.
Hikiwakuru is the second Cami alternative for sawing. The entry then introduces a poetic sense, with Per- continuing as perceber below.
Completes perceber, to perceive or understand. Waku kata mo nai illustrates being unable to make out or distinguish something.

runs.text: Não entender, ou não ter modo pera diſcernir,

lines.note: The Portuguese explains the example as not understanding, or lacking a means to discern. Its final clause is completed on the following row.
Completes the explanation as inability to consider something. The tilde in algũa is retained over u, and this short continuation remains separate from the next verb entry.
A different waku means boiling, then by extension springing or gushing forth. Its printed past form ita differs from aita in the preceding sawing verb.

runs.text: ou arrebentar como fonte de agoa. ¶ M

lines.note: Completes the springing-forth sense with a water source; arrebentar has b, not OCR h. Mu- begins mushi ga waku. Its M is visibly italic beside an upright u, unlike the upright M of Muxiga later in this column; this mixed type is preserved.
Completes mushi ga waku, insects appearing or breeding in something. Nacerem and nouo retain the printed historical spellings rather than modern nascerem and novo.
Completes the insect example, then gives yu ga waku, water boiling or becoming hot. The dark final glyph after Feruer is the article a, lost as punctuation by OCR, and belongs with agoa below.
Completes ferver a agoa na panella: water boiling in the pot or heating up. The historical spellings panella and aquentarſe are retained.

runs.text: Vaqiagari, u, atta. l, vaqitachi, u.

lines.note: Wakiagari and wakitachi name vigorous rising or bubbling in boiling. The abbreviated u forms are retained as printed rather than expanded into complete modern verbs.
Completes the gloss as water boiling in bubbles. The scan supports burbulhoẽs, with l and one marked e; OCR burbuihoẽes misread the ascender and inserted an extra vowel.
Wakiake no sode is equated with furisode in Ximo usage. These are sleeves open at the side, as the next rows explain; the Japanese terms retain their printed historical spelling and type.

runs.text: Mangas com aberturas dos Quimoens dos mi-

lines.note: The definition describes sleeves with openings on children's quimoens, garments whose name is borrowed from Japanese. Mi- begins mininos on the next line.
Completes mininos, children, retaining the historical vowel sequence. This short line belongs to the sleeve definition and is not a separate headword.
Wakibasami means carrying something tucked under the arm. The scan shows a small terminal division mark after sobra-, which continues as sobraçada below.
Completes sobraçada and illustrates carrying a tachi under the arm. Tachi wo wakibasamu is a Japanese example, followed by the Portuguese verb leuar.

runs.text: o montante de baixo do braço.

lines.note: Completes the example as carrying the large sword under one's arm. Montante is the dictionary's Portuguese description of the weapon here.

runs.text: Armas de de baixo dos braços.

lines.note: Wakibiki denotes armour protecting the area beneath the arms. The duplicated de de is visibly printed and is retained; baixo, not OCR barxo, supplies the location.
Wakikaeri describes water churning upward and returning downward. The printed principal part etta is retained as supplied, and the coordinated gloss continues below.

runs.text: tornar pera baixo como agoa quente, ou como

lines.note: The liquid returns downward as hot water does, or as in a second comparison continued below. This describes turbulent motion rather than a separate directional verb.
Completes the comparison with water falling from a height. The contiguous dalto and comma after agoa remain as printed.

runs.text: Idolos que eſtão à ilharga do prin-

lines.note: Wakidachi names attendant images standing beside a principal Buddhist figure. Prin- begins principal on the next physical row.
Completes principal Fotoque, the central Buddhist image flanked by attendants. Fotoque is a Japanese religious term inside the Portuguese explanation and remains in its printed italic type.
This second wakidachi entry cites wakidachi no mizu and directs the reader back to waki. It repeats the earlier water-depth expression, distinct from the attendant-image sense above.
Completes Vide Vaqi, the cross-reference to the earlier armpit-depth entry. The short upright word is body text, not a catchword.
Wakide means coming or gushing out, illustrated by underground water. The headword is followed by a comma before its principal parts; a- begins agoa below.

Completes agoa de baixo da terra, water emerging from beneath the earth. The scan reads goa rather than OCR gos, and baixo is wholly italic; the new example begins mushi ga wakizuru, with the final z doubled across the line break.
Completes wakizzuru, insects coming forth or being produced in quantity. The printed zz across the physical break is retained instead of modernizing the historical form.
Completes the insect example: coming out of something. The abbreviated dalgũa retains its printed tilde and remains a separate physical continuation.
Wakiga denotes offensive armpit odour. Enlargement supports cheiro in the close-set cheiroruim, rather than the OCR chxiro; the word spacing is preserved.
